images.alt: A black Oric Atmos home computer with a red stripe, photographed from the front showing its full keyboard
images.caption: The Atmos answered complaints about the Oric-1's hard calculator keys with a new case and a keyboard that actually moved.
images.author: Kerbdog

images.alt: An Oric Atmos computer shown at an angle, displaying its black case, red accent stripe and keyboard
images.caption: Built by Oric Products International in Cambridgeshire, the Atmos shipped in February 1984 with a 6502A and eight-colour graphics.
images.author: Unknown

images.alt: An Oric-1 and an Oric Atmos home computer photographed side by side, showing the case redesign between the two models
images.caption: The Atmos kept the Oric-1's 6502A and AY-3-8912 sound chip, but replaced the case and the keyboard reviewers had disliked.
images.author: Marcin Wichary from San Francisco, U.S.A.

images.alt: An Oric Atmos computer on display at a retro computing exhibition, shown with its keyboard and case
images.caption: Britain treated the Oric as a permanent runner-up to the Spectrum; in France it was sold as a first-class machine and became a phenomenon.
images.author: Soupmeister

images.alt: Close-up detail of an Oric Atmos computer's keyboard and case texture
images.caption: Oric BASIC gave the Atmos's better sound hardware four ready-made noises: ZAP, PING, SHOOT and EXPLODE.
images.author: Unknown
